history.ask: Situation at the moment of collapse
options: Prolonged standing, heat, crowding, or pain/fear/blood-draw
On standing up from sitting or lying
Nausea, sweating, vision greying out over seconds to minutes
No warning at all — sudden blackout
Limp, pale, still — recovered in under a minute
Jerking limbs for over a minute with tongue biting
Brief myoclonic jerks after falling (seconds only)
Confused or drowsy for more than 5 minutes
Woke with tongue laceration or urinary incontinence
Recurrent over years, always with typical triggers
Known structural heart disease or heart failure
Family history of sudden death < 40 years
Antihypertensives or diuretics (recently started or increased)
Poor oral intake / fasting in heat

history.ask: Symptoms just before or after the event
options: Sweating and hunger relieved by eating

red_flags: Syncope during exertion or while supine
Syncope preceded by palpitations or chest pain
Family history of sudden cardiac death under 40
Known structural heart disease, heart failure, or previous infarction
No prodrome at all — instantaneous collapse with facial injury
Signs of GI bleeding (melaena, haematemesis) with the collapse
New focal neurological deficit or severe sudden headache on waking
exam: Measure lying BP, then standing BP at 1 and 3 minutes — a drop ≥ 20 mmHg systolic (or ≥ 10 diastolic) confirms orthostatic hypotension
Palpate the pulse for rate, rhythm, and character — slow-rising and weak suggests aortic stenosis; irregular suggests AF
Auscultate for an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids (aortic stenosis)
Auscultate for other murmurs and listen at the apex in left lateral position
Look for pallor of conjunctivae and palmar creases, and check capillary refill (blood loss)
Perform a digital rectal exam if any suggestion of GI bleeding — melaena confirms the source of hypovolaemia
Examine tongue lateral borders for bite marks (seizure)
Screen neurological status: pupils, speech, limb power, gait — any focal deficit reroutes to stroke work-up
Inspect for injury pattern — facial/head injury without protective hand reflex suggests no prodrome (arrhythmic cause)
Estimate JVP and auscultate lungs — raised JVP with clear syncope raises massive PE or tamponade

investigations.why: The single highest-yield test — rules in arrhythmic substrate: bradycardia, AV block, long QT, pre-excitation, Brugada pattern, old infarction; LVH with strain supports aortic stenosis; sinus tachycardia with right-heart strain supports PE
Immediately rules hypoglycaemia in or out, especially in diabetics on insulin or sulfonylurea — a documented low value with symptom relief on eating settles the diagnosis
Low haemoglobin rules in blood loss / anaemia as the cause of orthostatic collapse — pairs with the melaena question and rectal exam
Dehydration (raised urea/creatinine) supports hypovolaemic orthostatic syncope; potassium, calcium and magnesium abnormalities predispose to the arrhythmias the ECG is screening for
Mandatory when a murmur, exertional syncope, or abnormal ECG is present — confirms or excludes aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and structural disease behind ventricular arrhythmia
For recurrent unexplained episodes with a normal resting ECG — catches intermittent AV block or paroxysmal tachyarrhythmia that a single tracing misses
Rules ectopic pregnancy in or out as the cause of hypovolaemic collapse in any woman of reproductive age with syncope and abdominal symptoms

Second-line — NOT routine for classic syncope; only if focal deficit, persistent confusion, severe sudden headache, or significant head injury from the fall — then it rules intracranial bleeding in or out
